Issued at 510 AM CDT Sat Oct 10 2026

Southwest flow aloft over the Northern Plains this morning as a
trough digging into the Pacific Northwest becomes positively-
tilted and stretched. A surface lee trough of low pressure is 
analyzed from southeast Saskatchewan along the MT/ND border. The
broad surface low will migrate eastward across the state this 
morning and afternoon. A relatively cooler air mass advecting in
behind the low will keep high temperatures in the mid 60s in 
far northwest North Dakota this afternoon, increasing 
southeastward to as warm as the mid 80s in the southern James 
River Valley where the cooler air mass is unlikely to reach 
until after peak heating.

Shortwave energy will begin ejecting northeastward from the 
base of the western trough this evening and continue through 
Monday. Meanwhile, colder air will continue filtering in from 
the north as the departing surface low evolves into a 
positively-tilted surface trough from Lake Superior to the 
Central Plains. Low to medium chances for light rain spread 
across the state from southwest to northeast late this evening 
through tonight. Higher chances then enter western North Dakota 
late Sunday morning, refocusing over northern North Dakota 
through Sunday afternoon. The highest chances for rain arrive 
Sunday night into Monday as a more well-defined shortwave 
reaches the Northern Great Plains under the right entrance 
region of an upper jet. Rain chances finally diminish Monday 
evening into Tuesday morning as the northern stream detaches 
from a cutoff low over Nevada, allowing mid level height rises 
to commence over the region as surface high pressure begins 
moving in from Montana. With this not being a strong dynamical 
system with only very low potential for mesoscale banding and 
poor mid level lapse rates, confidence is high in ensemble QPF 
output that places medium to high probabilities for exceeding 
half an inch of rain along and north of a line from the 
southwest corner of the state to the Turtle Mountains through 
Monday night. A 50 percent chance of exceeding a quarter of an 
inch of rain reach as far south as Hettinger, Bismarck, and 
Carrington. 

NBM distributions show increased confidence in the high and low
temperature forecast tonight through Monday. Lows tonight are 
projected to range from the mid 30s northwest to lower 50s 
southeast, with only a slight warmup to the mid 40s northwest to
lower 60s southeast for highs on Sunday. Sunday night lows fall
into the 30s. Given expected cloud cover, think it is more 
likely that Sunday night lows will end up on the warmer side of 
the NBM distribution, keeping the probability of sub-freezing 
temperatures low. One area that has a slightly higher chance of 
sub-freezing temperatures is northwest North Dakota, where both 
the NBM and CAMs reaching that forecast time range indicate a 
potential for rain briefly mixing with or changing over to snow.
Some very light snow accumulations (less than 1 inch) on grassy
surfaces cannot be ruled out, but snowfall rates are unlikely 
to be high enough to overcome warmer ground temperatures, and 
any snow that does accumulate should quickly melt by late Monday
morning. Under a cloudy sky with high precipitation chances, 
highs on Monday are only expected to reach the 40s. 

There is some potential for widespread below freezing 
temperatures Monday night, but there is also high confidence in 
an overcast sky prevailing. Temperatures may still be able to 
fall to around 30 degrees at some locations regardless, but the 
projected cloud cover limiting radiational cooling lowers 
confidence in a widespread freeze. Most areas should remain dry 
on Tuesday as broad surface high pressure roams through the 
region, with highs returning to the lower and mid 50s. 

Confidence in the evolution of the synoptic pattern mid to late
next week has lowered over the last 24 hours. Previous ensemble
cluster analyses projected as high as a 95 percent chance that 
the cutoff low at the base of the western CONUS trough would 
eject into the Plains and initiate a Colorado low, albeit with 
great uncertainty in its timing and track. Now though, it 
appears that there is anywhere from a 30 to 50 percent chance 
that the cutoff low never makes it east of the Rockies, or does 
so much later in the week, to the point that it never phases 
with a potent Canadian shortwave and either remains quasi-
stationary or tries to enter a ridging pattern before 
dissolving. The 00Z deterministic GFS and ECMWF paint the 
opposite ends of the forecast spectrum quite well, with the 
former simulating a powerful low with high chances for rain, 
strong winds, and wrap- around snow potential, and the latter 
keeping a mild and dry pattern with high pressure in place 
through the remainder of the week. The most likely outcome 
certainly falls somewhere between these two extremes, and is 
fairly well portrayed by the NBM with medium chances for rain
